items.why: The while-clause sharply contrasts the five men entering with the priest and soldiers remaining at the gate.
Two separate takings make the word “first” a meaningful temporal distinction.
“Our king” directly supplies the answer, while gods and humans concern the wine rather than rulership.
The causal clause supports the key, though the commonsense link between abundance and prosperity offers a shortcut.
It cleanly distinguishes the stated cause of the search from the nearby background fact about Israel’s king.
The explicit cause names Abimelek, whereas the citizens of Shechem enter the narrative only afterward.
The nested instruction clearly separates the relatives receiving the command from the citizens receiving the message.
It tests the distinction between the Levite’s purpose in leaving and the destination he later happens to reach.
The joy statement is a conditional wish rather than an obvious request, making the question’s wording strained.
“Does something” is vague and insubstantial, and the proposed competitor is not a plausible beneficiary.
It distinguishes the reported field movement that triggers the ambush from Abimelek’s later observation at the city.
The mother’s stated maker and the silversmith who actually makes the image form a strong intentional-versus-actual contrast.
The agent-patient relation is clear, but the servant’s death is not a very plausible misreading.
Fire is an obvious cause of death, while merely entering the stronghold is not a credible direct killer.
Adjacent duration clauses give two highly plausible endpoints for different activities.
The overtaking and shouting occur together, so either could reasonably be understood as prompting the turn.
The rhetorical refusal supplies the reason, while the move to the vine is clearly a subsequent event.
Approaching to burn the tower is also part of attacking it, so the competitor is broadly true.
The pronoun’s target distinguishes taking over the land from attacking its unsuspecting inhabitants.
The explicit causal statement supports the priestly relationship rather than the Levite’s nearby birthplace.
The route order is answerable, but the question is awkward and focuses on an incidental travel detail.
Resolving “him” to Jerub-Baal rather than nearby Abimelek tests a consequential antecedent relation.
It separates Zebul as secret sender from Gaal as the subject of the message.
It cleanly distinguishes the priest being asked from God as the source he is asked to consult.
The curse is not clearly subsequent to the punishment, and the competitor describes Abimelek rather than the people.
Zebul’s correction directly contrasts shadows with Gaal’s claimed people.
The purpose clause gives the result, though the competing anointing action belongs only to the following parable.
The olive tree’s rhetorical concern states its reason, while turning to the fig tree happens afterward.
The embedded “you” identifies Micah’s mother despite Micah being the current speaker.
The sequence clearly separates grape work in the fields from the festival meal during which they curse Abimelek.
The explicit isolation clause gives the cause, though ordinary common sense also strongly favors it.
